                                       PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §            PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                     §                    OF TEXAS


                        COMMENTS OF INFINIUM OPERATIONS, LLC

                                        I.   INTRODUCTION

       Infinium Operations, LLC and certain of its affiliates (“Infinium”) develops, owns, and

operates eFuels plants that convert hydrogen and waste CO₂ into low-carbon transportation fuels.

Such facilities may qualify as large loads due the power requirements of their electrolysis and fuel

synthesis facilities. Today, Infinium owns one eFuels plant operating in Corpus Christi. It is

working with project investors to construct another eFuels plant in Pecos and is developing other

projects across the State of Texas.

       Although we recognize the importance of evaluating early-stage projects for commercial

viability, Infinium is concerned that certain proposed approaches—particularly those related to

demonstrating site control and posting collateral—may inadvertently disadvantage industrial

developers. These measures create barriers to investment, particularly as it relates to projects that

are sensitive to early-stage development costs. Many of the proposed market design elements seek

to address issues created by the burgeoning data centers, but as drafted will impact other industrial

loads that also fall within the “large load” category.

       We appreciate the Commission’s effort on this rulemaking and consideration of the key

issues we identify below.
                            II.   RESPONSE TO DISCUSSION DRAFT

Financial Security Requirements:

        Requiring developers to post collateral before interconnect studies are completed presents

significant challenges for project development staging, particularly for large-load industrial and

energy projects. In early-stage development, well before a project reaches Final Investment

Decision (“FID”), developers typically do not have full financing in place. Instead, they rely on

limited early-stage capital to progress permitting, engineering, land options, environmental work,

and, critically, to obtain a detailed understanding of interconnect feasibility, cost, and schedule.

This interconnect visibility is one of the most important inputs to assessing overall project viability.

        Collateral represents one of the hardest forms of early stage capital to raise. It offers no

return on investment, carries high risk, and may be tied up for extended periods of time without

certainty that a proposed project will meet final investment criteria. A requirement to post high

levels of collateral too early will chill investment in infrastructure projects in Texas through the

diversion of scarce development capital away from essential feasibility work and increases the

financial burden during a period when the project has the least certainty and the fewest committed

partners.

        For large-load projects, interconnection costs and timelines can materially impact the

viability of a site or even the overall project concept. Developers must first understand whether

interconnection is technically feasible, whether infrastructure upgrades are required, how long

those upgrades will take, and what the associated costs will be. These factors directly affect project

economics, sequencing, and financing strategy. Requiring collateral before this information is

available forces developers to take on disproportionate financial risk without the foundational data

needed to justify the commitment.
        In effect, early collateral posting creates a development paradox: developers are asked to

secure high-risk capital commitments before they have the technical and economic information

needed to secure financing or even determine whether the project is feasible. This misalignment

in staging can significantly hinder project advancement, deter capital providers, and ultimately

reduce the number of viable projects that progress to construction—particularly in regions where

interconnection uncertainty is already a key barrier.

       A more practical approach is to require a more modest upfront collateral amount prior to

initiating studies. If the project proceeds, this amount may be applied as CIAC or returned when

CIAC is paid. If the project does not move forward, the collateral is returned minus a reasonable

service fee to cover study administration. This structure still ensures developer commitment while

right-sizing early-stage risk. It also naturally clears out stalled or non-viable projects, as those

developers will request the return of their collateral—signaling that the project will not advance—

thereby improving queue hygiene without deterring serious investment.

       We also suggest considering a tiered approach to the collateral sizing, whereby loads less

than 500MW would be required to post $5,000/MW, and loads greater than 500MW would be

required to post $20,000/MW. Until very recently, 500 MW was considered a very large project,

and would be a clear benchmark to distinguish between industrial loads like Infinium and projects

so large that they are referred to as “hyper” scale.
 Site Control:

       For large-load projects, certainty around interconnection feasibility, costs, and schedule is

a critical prerequisite to committing to full site control through a binding purchase or long-term

lease. In standard development practice, a project begins with a land option agreement that grants

temporary rights to evaluate the property while limiting upfront financial exposure. During this

option period, developers complete essential due diligence—most importantly, understanding the

interconnect potential, associated upgrade costs, and realistic timing of grid access.

       Because interconnection results can materially alter project viability, it is common for

developers to pivot to an alternative site if the study reveals prohibitive constraints or costs.

Forcing full site control before an interconnect study is conducted creates a classic “chicken-and-

egg” problem: developers must commit significant capital to control a site without knowing

whether the location is even feasible from a grid-integration standpoint. This requirement can

distort normal development sequencing, elevate financial risk, and ultimately discourage

investment in the region, particularly for projects with large and complex interconnection

footprints.

       Allowing developers to hold an option to acquire or to lease land to demonstrate site

control is consistent with industry-standard practice and is economically rational. It

ensures that landowners, utilities, and developers make decisions based on validated

technical information while supporting responsible project advancement and reducing the

likelihood of stranded investment or abandoned sites.
 Developer and End-User Distinction:

       Finally, the distinction between a “developer” and an “end-user” is not a meaningful

indicator of whether a project will ultimately move forward. Regardless of who develops the

project, success is driven by fundamental project economics and the presence of credible,

committed customers.

       For example, Infinium is the original developer of Project Roadrunner, a large-load eFuels

facility in West Texas. When the project reached FID, it was financed by industry leading

infrastructure partners, with Infinium retaining a minority interest. Project Roadrunner is currently

under construction and is slated to produce sustainable aviation fuel that will be sold to major

airlines under long-term supply contracts which contracts support the projects investment.

       What enabled this project to advance was not the type of entity advancing development of

the project, but rather the quality of the development work, the strength of the project economics,

and the secured offtake agreements.

       In applying these requirements, customers and project sponsors alike would benefit from

clear expectations around process and timing. Given the significant costs, risks, and administrative

responsibilities associated with the proposal, it is important that these obligations be paired with

transparency in procedures, evaluation criteria, outcomes, and—critically—the timelines for

completing studies and issuing decisions. A predictable and well-communicated process will help

support meaningful investment and give viable projects the confidence needed to move forward.
                                     III.   CONCLUSION

       We appreciate Commission staff’s consideration of these issues and look forward to

collaborating on this rulemaking.

                                                Respectfully submitted,

                                                  X
                                                Liz Myers
                                                SVP, Strategy & Solutions
                                                Infinium Operations, LLC
                                                lmyers@infiniumco.com
